models.summary: Four named island states, the Maldives, Tuvalu, Kiribati and the Marshall Islands, 584,408 people on 1,316 square kilometres, stand in for all small island developing states and are collapsed into one cone. The cone has a base of 444 square kilometres, a radius of 20 kilometres and a height of 2 metres. Sea level rises in a straight line at 3.44 mm a year, read from altimetry. The slope is height over radius, so the flooded radius at each year follows from the rise, the drowned area is the ring between the two radii, and the new displaced that year are the density times the newly drowned area. Density itself grows at a fixed 2.3 percent a year from 444 people per square kilometre, and does not depend on height or radius. People cannot retreat inland, so everyone in the flooded band is sent abroad. One cone is scaled to the world by the stated 65 million island-state residents in 2070. The sum over 50 years is 18,230,968.

models.summary: The fifty largest emitters from 1970 to 2018, who produced 89.7 percent of emissions, are the candidate receivers. Four indicators are weighted by the entropy method: greenhouse gas emissions, arable land per person, product per person, and renewable freshwater per person. Each country's share of an indicator is its value over the column sum, the entropy is minus a constant times the sum of share times log share, and the weight is the normalized one-minus-entropy. The weights come out 0.259, 0.239, 0.139 and 0.363. The paper checks them against expectation: land and water sustain life and emissions measure blame, so the result is called reliable. Scoring and ranking gives a top twenty, who produced 74.6 percent of emissions and are assigned the duty. Canada, Australia and the United States lead at 0.163, 0.121 and 0.120.

models.summary: Culture is treated as a species. The share of people carrying it is its population, zero means extinct, and one hundred percent is the ceiling. A foreign culture competes with the native one for the same resources, population, language and geography, exactly as an invading species would. The model is the two-species Lotka-Volterra competition system. For Canada the population is fit by a logistic curve to 3.8 times 10 to the 7 in 2070, and the first two models send 2.97 million newcomers there, so the shares start at 92.7 and 7.3 percent. With no protection the native culture uses resources better, so the foreign culture's effect on it is smaller than the reverse. With the protection policy the two effects are set roughly equal, and the comparison of the two figures shows the newcomers' culture surviving longer.

models.summary: For each receiving country the yearly effect is the value the displaced create minus what the state spends on them. Newcomers cost a resettlement payment once and a living cost every year. They create nothing in the first year, following the rule that resettlement support lasts one year, and after that each working one creates 0.75 of the host's product per person. The share able to work is the world share aged 15 to 64, 65.33 percent, and everyone who can work does. Costs do not vary with age, sex or background. Table 4 prices twenty countries. Run over fifty years the curves split: Canada, Australia and the United States cross from loss to gain in a little over two years and finish above five billion; most developing countries stay in deficit the whole way.
